maintained_by: Hand-maintained. Update bill statuses from the Connecticut General Assembly bill status pages; every entry cites its source.
disclaimer: Research support for residents, families and advocates. Listing a bill here is not an endorsement or a position of the Connecticut Long Term Care Ombudsman Program; official positions come from the State Long Term Care Ombudsman.

session.date_note: Computed from the constitutional schedule: the Wednesday after the first Monday in January, adjourning by the Wednesday after the first Monday in June. Committee deadlines are set by the joint rules each session; add them when the General Assembly publishes them.

topics.name: Staffing and workforce
topics.why: Staffing levels shape how quickly residents get help, how care is planned and whether residents are treated with dignity. Connecticut's standard is 3.00 direct-care hours per resident per day, of which 0.84 licensed. Proposals to raise it to 4.10 (2023 SB 1026) and 3.60 (2025 SB 1279) did not pass. The federal minimum staffing rule was repealed by CMS in December 2025, so the state standard is the main numeric floor.

context_facts.text: A May 2025 state agreement with SEIU 1199NE set a pathway to $26 per hour for nursing home CNAs by January 1, 2028.

CMS repealed the 2024 federal nursing home minimum staffing rule (3.48 total hours, 0.55 RN hours, 24/7 RN) through an interim final rule released December 2, 2025. The facility assessment requirement remains.
context_facts.source_title: LeadingAge, CMS repeals nursing home minimum staffing standards

questions: How many residents live in homes below the current standard, and for how many quarters in a row?
What would a higher standard cost, and how would it be paid for through Medicaid rates?
How are temporary agency staff counted, and do they cover the shortfall?
What happens to residents when a home misses the standard: who checks, and how often?

topics.name: Quality, inspections and oversight
topics.why: Inspections and penalties are how the state and CMS respond when care falls short. Recent laws raised DPH civil penalties (PA 25-96) and added training and monitoring rights (PA 26-28, PA 26-44).
questions: Are inspection frequency and staffing at DPH enough to find problems early?
Are penalties large enough, and are they collected and reinvested for residents?
How quickly do residents and families learn about serious citations at their home?

topics.name: Ownership, finance and Medicaid rates
topics.why: Who owns a home and how public money flows affect staffing and stability. PA 26-103 begins investment-entity ownership reporting in February 2027. The 2026 budget act began phasing in the federal PDPM payment model and performance payments.

context_facts.text: Connecticut's average Medicaid case mix index (resident acuity used in rate setting) rose from 0.9591 in Q1 2021 to 1.1270 in Q1 2025, about 17.5%.

questions: What will the first investment-entity reports (due Feb 15, 2027) show, and will they be public?
How are Medicaid rate increases tied to direct care, wages and staffing?
How do related-party payments (rent, management fees) compare with spending on care?

topics.name: Discharge, transfer and resident rights
topics.why: Discharge and eviction are among the most frequent complaints the Ombudsman program receives. Recent laws changed notice and appeal rules (PA 23-48, PA 25-16) and banned discrimination in long-term care settings (PA 25-17).

context_facts.text: The Ombudsman program's FFY 2025 report names fear of retaliation as an ongoing barrier to raising concerns in every long-term care setting.

questions: Are discharge notices reaching the Ombudsman program in time for residents to appeal?
Where do residents go after an involuntary discharge, and how often is it a shelter or hospital?
What protections against retaliation exist, and are they working?

topics.name: Closures, capacity and emergencies
topics.why: Closures and evacuations uproot residents. The two-bed room limit for new placements began July 1, 2026 (PA 24-141), and 2026 laws changed the bed moratorium and certificate-of-need rules (PA 26-74).
questions: How much notice do residents get before a closure, and who helps them choose a new home?
Will the two-bed limit reduce available beds in some regions?
Which homes are near the end of their building's useful life?

topics.name: Residential care homes and assisted living
topics.why: Thousands of people live in residential care homes and assisted living, settings with fewer federal protections than nursing homes. 2026 laws added virtual monitoring in residential care homes (PA 26-28), fear-of-retaliation training in assisted living (PA 26-44), hearings on large assisted living fee increases (PA 26-74) and a working group on licensing managed residential communities (PA 26-13).
questions: Should managed residential communities be licensed, and what would licensing cover?
How are residents protected from large fee increases and evictions?
What data does the state collect on complaints and incidents in these settings?

topics.name: Ombudsman program capacity
topics.why: The Long Term Care Ombudsman Program is how residents raise concerns without fear. Its reach depends on staff, volunteers and appropriations; the FFY 2025 report says the Community Ombudsman program's scope was limited by staffing and appropriations.
questions: How many residents can each Ombudsman reasonably serve, and how does Connecticut compare?
What would it take to visit every facility regularly?
How is the Community Ombudsman program funded for home and community settings?

topics.name: Aging, long-term care financing and conservatorship
topics.why: Connecticut is aging, and how people pay for long-term care shapes where they can live. 2026 laws added long-term care insurance safeguards (PA 26-93) and conservatorship changes (PA 26-87).

context_facts.text: About one in five Connecticut residents (20.4%) is 65 or older.
Nearly 100,000 people in Connecticut have long-term care insurance; a CT Mirror review found more than 17,000 faced rate increases of 50% or more between January 2019 and October 2024.

questions: Does the personal needs allowance keep up with costs? (2026 HB 5300 proposed a cost-of-living adjustment and was not enacted.)
How are conservators trained and overseen?
What happens to residents who outlive their long-term care insurance or savings?

bills_past.title: An Act Concerning the Use of Technology for Virtual Monitoring in Residential Care Homes
bills_past.summary: Allows residents of residential care homes to use their own technology for virtual monitoring of their rooms, with notice, written roommate consent in shared rooms, and a seven-day advance written notice to the home. Also adjusts the existing liability immunity for nursing homes and extends similar immunity to residential care homes.
bills_past.last_action: Signed by the Governor May 20, 2026 (Public Act 26-28 issued May 14, 2026)
bills_past.notes: Setting named in the bill title and status page is residential care homes only (not assisted living/MRC). Section 2 amends the existing nursing home technology immunity statute (OLR describes the act as covering RCHs and nursing homes). The act itself sets no individual fines; the status page statement of purpose says it 'prescribes a penalty' but the act text summary describes home-initiated action for noncompliance with an appeal process. The Long-Term Care Ombudsman may publish standard forms; the DPH commissioner may adopt regulations. Pre-existing nursing home virtual monitoring law is PA 21-55 (SB 975, 2021) per LTCOP page.
bills_past.short_title: Virtual monitoring (cameras) in residential care homes

bills_past.title: An Act Requiring Nursing Homes to Annually Report Certain Ownership Information Regarding Investment Entities
bills_past.summary: Requires nursing homes to report annually to DSS on investment entities holding at least a 5% beneficial interest, starting February 15, 2027, and to attest to DPH beginning February 1, 2028 that the licensee controls the home and no investment entity controls resident care. Sets a DSS fine of $1,000 per day for late or missing reports and a DPH civil penalty of up to $2,000 per attestation violation, and may require a surety bond or similar security from July 1, 2028 if DSS identifies a feasible instrument.

key_dates.what: First annual investment-entity ownership reports due to DSS
DSS to notify homes of any feasible security instrument; if none identified, bond requirement does not take effect
Licensee control requirement and annual attestation to DPH begin
DSS report to Aging, Appropriations, Human Services and Public Health committees due
Bond/security (90 days of operating costs) required for covered homes at initial license or renewal, if DSS identifies a feasible instrument

bills_past.last_action: Signed by the Governor June 4, 2026 (Public Act 26-103 issued May 19, 2026)

sources.title: CT Mirror: nursing home oversight bill clears final hurdle

bills_past.notes: It is Senate Bill 125 (not HB). The surety bond is conditional: it applies only if DSS identifies a feasible security instrument (surety bond, escrow, insurance product), so avoid describing it as an unconditional requirement. Waiver applications must be filed at least six months before the compliance deadline; waivers last one year. R-0080 table lists 'October 1, 2026; reporting requirement upon passage' for effective dates. Senate passed May 4, House passed May 6, 2026.
bills_past.short_title: Nursing home investment-entity ownership reporting

bills_past.title: An Act Concerning Fear of Retaliation Training for Persons Providing Assisted Living Services in Managed Residential Communities
bills_past.summary: Requires each assisted living services agency serving a managed residential community to provide annual in-service training to employees on residents' fear of retaliation for complaints about their care, including residents' right to file complaints, examples of retaliatory conduct, and ways to prevent retaliation.
bills_past.last_action: Signed by the Governor May 20, 2026 (Public Act 26-44 issued May 14, 2026)
bills_past.notes: Bill number HB 5141 confirmed. Trainer need not be a qualified social worker or social worker consultant, per OLR summary (R01 version of the summary).
bills_past.short_title: Fear-of-retaliation training in assisted living

bills_past.title: An Act Concerning Various Revisions to Human Services Statutes
bills_past.summary: Among other provisions, requires managed residential communities to post DSS contact information for reporting suspected elder abuse or neglect with their residents' bill of rights, incorporates two federal nursing home rules on psychotropic drugs and resident participation in treatment, and revises the Long-Term Care Planning Committee and Advisory Council. Also requires annual DSS HUSKY C reports from 2027 through 2032.

key_dates.what: Effective for most provisions listed (MRC posting, federal regulations, LTC Planning Committee/Advisory Council)
First annual DSS HUSKY C report due (continues through Oct 1, 2032)

bills_past.last_action: Signed by the Governor June 2, 2026 (Public Act 26-72 issued May 19, 2026)
bills_past.notes: Bill number HB 5562 confirmed. The OLR summary is internally inconsistent on the Long-Term Care Planning Committee report deadline (header says January 1, 2027; body says January 1, 2028); do not publish a deadline for it without checking the act text. Federal rules incorporated as of Jan 1, 2026: 42 CFR 483.45(e) and 483.10(c). Act also covers unrelated items (wheelchair repair council, LGBTQ network, etc.).
bills_past.short_title: Human services revisions (MRC bill of rights, federal resident rights)

bills_past.title: An Act Concerning Assisted Living Rate-Increase Hearings, Municipal Agents for Aging, Generator Requirements, Home Health Aide PPE, the Nursing Home Bed Moratorium, and Nursing Home Data
bills_past.summary: Requires an informational hearing at least 30 days before an assisted living services agency fee increase above 10%. Adds an exception to the nursing home bed moratorium allowing DSS to approve new Medicaid-certified beds (preference for small-house-style homes) and revises certificate-of-need criteria, and creates a separate DSS audit process for nursing home minimum data set (MDS) information.

key_dates.what: MDS audit provisions effective; municipal agent conflict-of-interest certification begins
Bed moratorium exception and CON criteria effective upon passage (Public Act issued)

bills_past.last_action: Signed by the Governor May 27, 2026 (Public Act 26-74 issued May 19, 2026)
bills_past.notes: Bill number is SB 123 (not SB 288). The bed moratorium and MDS/resident data provisions overlap in subject with SB 288 (not enacted), but no source opened states that SB 288 was formally folded in; SB 288's related-party employee reimbursement cap provision does not appear in the OLR summary of PA 26-74. Bed-need standard changed to occupancy above 96% for two consecutive quarters (previously 97.5% projected over five years), with DSS to consider bed need within 15 miles and the requesting home's CMS five-star rating. The 'upon passage' effective date for sections 5-6 is as stated by OLR; the date shown is the PA issue date, not a separately stated effective date. Section 2 (municipal agents for aging, conflict-of-interest certification) corresponds in subject to SB 124 (2026, not enacted separately). MDS documentation response time is 10 days (vs 30 for other audits).
bills_past.short_title: Assisted living fee hearings, bed moratorium, MDS audits

bills_past.title: An Act Making Adjustments to the State Budget for the Biennium Ending June 30, 2027
bills_past.summary: State budget adjustment act. Long-term care provisions listed by OLR include new performance-based and high-Medicaid-mix nursing home payments with a PDPM phase-in beginning July 1, 2026, repeal of the scheduled 6% quarterly nursing home revenue tax (existing user fees retained), exclusion of nursing home directors/assistant directors from scheduled wage increases, a DPH two-bed-limit waiver for one home per small-house skilled nursing facility through July 1, 2027, a family caregiver tax credit, an aging-in-place grant program, and MOLST form changes.

key_dates.what: PDPM phase-in begins; small-house two-bed waiver provision effective

bills_past.last_action: Signed by the Governor May 26, 2026 (Public Act 26-68 issued May 14, 2026)

sources.title: LCO Public and Special Acts by Number

bills_past.notes: PA 26-68 is the budget adjustment bill SB 1 (not the 'implementer'). The implementer-type bill is SB 477 / PA 26-76 (separate entry), which amends PA 26-68 (sections 42-44 relate to nursing homes). Section cites from OLR: tax repeal sections 60-61; MOLST section 192; wage-increase exclusion section 445 (as amended by PA 26-76 section 42); Medicaid payments sections 446-447; two-bed waiver section 451; family caregiver credit section 271 (starts tax year 2027); aging-in-place grants section 343 (up to $10,000). Section-level effective dates are as stated in OLR report; the 'upon passage' items were not individually dated.
bills_past.short_title: Budget adjustments (nursing home rates, PDPM, provider tax repeal)

bills_past.title: An Act Concerning the Failure to File for Certain Grand List Exemptions, a Municipal Option to Abate Delinquent Property Taxes, State Fund Allocations, and Budget Implementation (biennium ending June 30, 2027)
bills_past.summary: Budget implementation act that amends PA 26-68 nursing home provisions: modifies the wage-increase exclusion for nursing home directors, lets DSS set bed need at a lower occupancy level for projects relocating beds to meet the two-bed limit, and waives the two-bed limit for certain nursing homes serving people transitioning from correction or DMHAS services.
bills_past.last_action: Signed by the Governor May 27, 2026 (Public Act 26-76 issued May 14, 2026)
bills_past.notes: Added because it amends PA 26-68. The OLR reports cite sections 42, 43, 44 and 77-78 (unlicensed facility penalty provisions). Sections 43-44 take effect upon passage per R-0080.
bills_past.short_title: Budget implementer (nursing home wage and two-bed limit changes)

bills_past.title: An Act Concerning Consumer Safeguards for Long-Term Care Policies
bills_past.summary: Requires long-term care insurers to report incurred and paid losses to the Insurance Commissioner each May 1, with annual aggregated, de-identified commissioner reports starting by October 1, 2027. Authorizes the commissioner to investigate suspected violations and impose corrective action plans, administrative remedies or penalties of up to $15,000, and allows an optional feasibility report on possible requirements such as refunds on rate increases above inflation.

key_dates.what: Optional commissioner feasibility report due (within available appropriations)
Commissioner's annual loss data reports begin

bills_past.last_action: Signed by the Governor June 2, 2026 (Public Act 26-93 issued May 19, 2026)

sources.title: CT Mirror: long-term care insurance legislation passed

bills_past.notes: Bill number SB 478 confirmed. CT Mirror says the state attorney general gets power to investigate insurers; the OLR summary says the Insurance Commissioner investigates and may refer suspected violations to the attorney general. This entry follows OLR. House vote 146-4 on May 5, 2026 per CT Mirror.
bills_past.short_title: Long-term care insurance consumer safeguards

bills_past.summary: Bars health care providers, including long-term care facilities, from discriminating against individuals receiving care, per LTCOP's summary.
bills_past.last_action: Signed by the Governor July 8, 2025 (Public Act 25-154 designated June 17, 2025)
bills_past.notes: Act text not read.
bills_past.short_title: Ban on discrimination by health care providers

bills_past.title: An Act Concerning Various Measures Recognizing and Honoring the Military Service of Veterans and Members of the Armed Forces in Connecticut
bills_past.summary: Veterans' military service recognition act that, per LTCOP's summary, gives priority admission to veterans seeking federally contracted veterans' nursing homes.
bills_past.last_action: Signed by the Governor June 3, 2025 (Public Act 25-15 issued May 30, 2025)
bills_past.notes: Nursing home provision relies on LTCOP's description; act text not read.
bills_past.short_title: Veterans measures (priority admission to VA-contracted nursing homes)

bills_past.title: An Act Concerning Nursing Home Staffing Ratios
bills_past.summary: As reported by the Aging Committee, would have raised the minimum nurse staffing level from 3.0 to 3.6 hours of direct care per resident per day effective July 1, 2026 (the original draft also had a 4.1-hour step on July 1, 2028, removed in the committee substitute). Tabled on the Senate calendar.

key_dates.what: Favorable report, tabled for the calendar, Senate (Calendar 108)

bills_past.last_action: Tabled for the Senate calendar March 18, 2025; no further action recorded
bills_past.notes: Not enacted. CT Mirror (Apr 28, 2025) estimated the cost at about $24M (headline: 'Boosting CT nursing home direct care would cost $24M'); that article was not opened.
bills_past.short_title: Nursing home staffing ratios (3.6 hours)

bills_past.title: An Act Promoting Nursing Home Resident Quality of Life
bills_past.summary: Bars nursing homes from placing newly admitted residents in rooms with more than two beds after July 1, 2026 (Class B violation, up to $10,000 per violation), requires admission of certain residents from closing homes, ends new rest home with nursing supervision licenses, expands DPH/DSS enforcement and management company certificate oversight (5% beneficial ownership disclosure), and adds MRC and ALSA fee disclosure rules.

key_dates.what: MRC and ALSA fee disclosure provisions effective
Two-bed limit working group report due
Newly admitted residents may not be placed in rooms with more than two beds

bills_past.last_action: Signed by the Governor June 4, 2024 (Public Act 24-141 issued May 22, 2024)

sources.title: Wiggin and Dana 2024 summary of key CT elder services legislation
CT Mirror: nursing home bill passes House

bills_past.notes: July 1, 2026 date confirmed by Wiggin summary and CT Mirror (a Vote Smart page title says 2027; not relied on). The Wiggin summary does not itself name HB 5046; the HB 5046 = PA 24-141 mapping comes from the bill status PDF. PA 26-68 section 451 later lets DPH waive the limit for one home per small-house skilled nursing facility through July 1, 2027, and PA 26-76 section 44 waives it for certain homes serving people transitioning from correction or DMHAS services. Existing residents in multi-bed rooms need not move (CT Mirror, describing the bill as passed by the House).
bills_past.short_title: Nursing home resident quality of life (two-bed room limit)

bills_past.title: An Act Supporting Connecticut Seniors and the Improvement of Nursing and Home-Based Care
bills_past.summary: Omnibus aging act creating a home care provider registry, links to Medicare Care Compare, a DPH nursing home consumer dashboard and Centers of Excellence program, presumptive Medicaid eligibility for home care, ombudsman-related notice and records access changes for ALSAs and MRCs, an MRC consumer guide, and mandatory municipal agents for the elderly.

key_dates.what: Centers of Excellence, nursing home dashboard and presumptive eligibility provisions effective

bills_past.last_action: Signed by the Governor May 21, 2024 (Public Act 24-39 issued May 14, 2024)
bills_past.notes: Wiggin summary does not name bill numbers; mapping from bill status PDF.
bills_past.short_title: Supporting seniors and nursing and home-based care

bills_past.title: An Act Concerning the Health and Safety of Connecticut Residents
bills_past.summary: Omnibus health and safety act including workplace violence prevention standards for certain Medicaid-reimbursed facilities including nursing homes, a definition of 'direct care' for nursing home staffing minimums, and a bar on nursing homes denying admission solely because an applicant received mental health services.
bills_past.last_action: Signed by the Governor May 21, 2024
bills_past.notes: The 'direct care' definition (section 31) took effect May 21, 2024 per Wiggin summary.
bills_past.short_title: Health and safety of residents (workplace violence, isolation)

bills_past.title: An Act Concerning Nursing Home Waiting Lists
bills_past.summary: Allows electronic nursing home waiting lists (required by July 1, 2025), sets rules for placing applicants on the list and documenting passed-over applicants, and gives DSS or the Long-Term Care Ombudsman access to investigate admission complaints.
bills_past.last_action: Signed by the Governor May 14, 2024 (Public Act 24-17 issued May 8, 2024)
bills_past.notes: Wiggin summary does not name the bill number; mapping from bill status PDF.
bills_past.short_title: Nursing home waiting lists

bills_past.title: An Act Concerning Notice of a Proposed Involuntary Transfer or Discharge of a Nursing Facility Resident, Family Councils in Managed Residential Communities, Coordination of Dementia Services, Nursing Home Transparency and Homemaker-Companion Agencies
bills_past.summary: Addresses involuntary transfer and discharge notices, family councils in managed residential communities, a dementia services coordinator, nursing home financial transparency, and homemaker-companion agency jurisdiction.
bills_past.last_action: Signed by the Governor June 13, 2023 (Public Act 23-48 issued June 6, 2023)
bills_past.notes: Effective dates not captured.
bills_past.short_title: Involuntary transfer and discharge notices, family councils, transparency

bills_past.title: An Act Concerning the Department of Public Health's Recommendations Regarding Change in Ownership of Health Care Facilities
bills_past.summary: Change of ownership review for health care facilities.
bills_past.last_action: Signed by the Governor June 27, 2023 (Public Act 23-122 issued June 15, 2023)
bills_past.notes: Act text not read.
bills_past.short_title: Change of ownership review for health care facilities

bills_past.title: An Act Concerning Nursing Home Staffing Ratios
bills_past.summary: Would have raised the minimum daily direct care hours per resident from 3 to 4.1, phased in by January 2026, per CT Mirror. Reported favorably by the Aging Committee and tabled on the Senate calendar.

key_dates.what: Favorable report, tabled for the calendar, Senate (Calendar 77)

bills_past.last_action: Tabled for the Senate calendar March 15, 2023; no further action recorded

sources.title: CT Mirror: elder care nursing home reform bills (May 8, 2023)

bills_past.notes: Not enacted. The 4.1-hour figure comes from CT Mirror; the Aging Committee JFR text read does not state hours (it mentions 4.1 only as a 2000 federal study cited by Connecticut Legal Services). CT Mirror reported a working group would study staffing instead.
bills_past.short_title: Nursing home staffing ratios (4.1 hours)

how_to.title: Find and follow a bill
how_to.text: Each bill has a status page on cga.ct.gov listing every action, the bill text, the fiscal note and the public hearing testimony. Search by number on the General Assembly home page.

how_to.title: Testify at a public hearing
how_to.text: Committees post hearing notices with instructions for registering to speak and submitting written testimony. Most hearings accept remote testimony. Watch the committee's page, especially Aging, Human Services, Public Health and Appropriations.

how_to.title: Using these numbers
how_to.text: Quote the number with its period and source, as shown on each card. Staffing figures are screening estimates from payroll data, not DPH findings. A resident's own story, shared with their consent, is often the most persuasive testimony.
